title: The Cash Buffer Number Most Owner-Led Businesses Have Never Actually Calculated
linkedin:
Most business owners can tell you the cash balance that feels safe. Almost none can tell you how they arrived at it.

It is usually a gut feel, a number the account once dropped to during a bad patch, or "three months of expenses" borrowed from a personal finance article and never actually tested against the business itself.

That guess goes wrong in two directions.

Run too thin and every predictable seasonal dip becomes a fresh emergency, pushing owners toward defensive decisions: delaying a supplier payment, knocking back a good contract because there is no room to fund it, reaching for expensive short-term finance exactly when their bargaining position is weakest.

Run too thick and the surplus sits idle, earning almost nothing in a transaction account, quietly forfeiting a return the business could be generating elsewhere. Most owners carrying a large buffer have never been asked to justify the number, which is usually the clearest sign it was never calculated.

The fix is not a rule of thumb. It is going back through twelve to twenty four months of actual bank movements, not the smoothed monthly figures in the P&L, and finding the real low point relative to the typical balance. That gap is the evidence. The buffer should sit comfortably above it.

It is also worth asking whether the whole buffer needs to be cash at all. A properly sized standby facility can cover part of that risk for the cost of interest only when it is drawn, instead of tying up cash year round.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Quick question for business owners: if we asked right now how much cash should be sitting in your account, could you explain how you got to that number, or is it just a figure that feels safe?

Most owners cannot say much beyond a gut feel, or a balance the account once dropped to during a scare.

The businesses that get this right are not holding more cash. They have actually measured how far their own account swings between a good month and a rough one, and sized the buffer to that gap instead of a generic rule of thumb.

Worth a real look next time you are checking the balance out of habit rather than reviewing it on purpose.
